implementation_notes: Node ships no persistence layer, so the token comes from the dominant data libraries: Sequelize supports optimistic locking through a model version count (the version is checked whenever the instance is modified and an OptimisticLockError is raised when the counts differ), while Mongoose documents carry a version key (__v by default) that save() compares when optimisticConcurrency is enabled on the schema. Both replace the hand-written predicate with a framework-managed counter - the classic form survives only in driver-level code (pg/mysql2), where you keep WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2 and test result.rowCount yourself. Whichever route is taken, the conflict decision (reload and retry, merge, or answer 409) stays in the application.
pitfalls: Mongoose's updateOne()/findOneAndUpdate()/findByIdAndUpdate() bypass document versioning; only save() honours optimisticConcurrency, so those query helpers need their own version filter.
Sequelize's counter participates only when the instance is saved through the model; bulk updates and raw queries skip it.
Catching the conflict and retrying with the same in-memory document re-writes the stale copy - re-read first.
Mongoose's __v also backs its default array/positional update behaviour, so renaming the versionKey or excluding paths changes both mechanisms at once.

variants.name: Mongoose document version key with optimistic concurrency
variants.implementation_notes: In a document store the token is the document revision: Mongoose maintains __v, and enabling optimisticConcurrency makes save() match the version it loaded and reject a document that changed underneath (the same shape as CouchDB revisions or an ETag). The document model replaces the row version column with no schema migration, but the check lives in document middleware - so query-level updates and bulk writes must add their own version filter. Choose it when MongoDB is the store; keep the SQL counter variant when the application persists to a relational database.
pitfalls: VersionError is only thrown by save(); collection-level helpers (bulkWrite, updateMany) ignore the document version.
Stripping __v from serialized responses is fine, but round-tripping a client's stale __v back into a hydrated document can hide the conflict.
